issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home' implies an interpersonal/home-intrusion threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items, which center on contamination/body danger and intrusive sensory reliving.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' is not impossible after chemical exposure, but here it reads as preparation for assault/entrapment rather than avoidance of fumes, contamination, or bodily symptoms; it is weakly aligned with the rest of the profile and the trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items focus strongly on social/cultural disconnection and not belonging, which is difficult to reconcile as the central appraisal pattern for a 60-year-old male whose trauma was toxic chemical exposure. These appraisals are not impossible, but alongside the rest of the profile they are poorly connected to the main symptom pattern of somatic threat, false alarms, and sensory reliving. A clinician would question why chemically exposure-related PTSD is expressed mainly as community/cultural alienation rather than danger, contamination, mistrust of body, or permanent harm beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the profile is dominated by body-based threat and intrusive sensory memory, but the maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others' is not well supported because the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from all other nodes. Reminder-based avoidance centered on external prompts by others implies a trigger-driven maintenance pattern that is not reflected in the formulation or elsewhere in the self-report.

vignette:
Thanh is a 60-year-old Vietnamese-American man who has managed a mid-sized hotel in the Pacific Northwest for nearly two decades. He lives with his long-term partner and was, by all accounts, a steady and capable professional - the kind of man who prided himself on knowing every corner of his building and keeping things running without incident. That self-image collapsed approximately fourteen months ago when a contractor improperly stored and mixed industrial cleaning chemicals in a poorly ventilated basement utility room. Thanh, conducting his customary morning walkthrough, entered the room and within seconds felt a searing burn in his throat and nasal passages, his eyes streaming, his chest tightening as if gripped from the inside. He stumbled backward into the corridor, unable to call out, certain in those moments that his lungs were being destroyed. Emergency services were called; he was hospitalised overnight for chemical inhalation injury. The physical damage was assessed as moderate and largely resolved within weeks. What did not resolve was everything else.

In the months that followed, the memory of those moments in the utility room began returning in a form that felt nothing like ordinary recollection. Without warning - during a staff briefing, while reviewing invoices, while simply walking the hotel's corridors - the memory would force itself into Thanh's mind with an immediacy that erased the present. He would feel the burn again at the back of his throat, and, most disturbingly, he could taste it: a sharp, acrid chemical taste that arrived with the memory as though it were still happening. He has described these intrusions as not remembering but returning - the sensation that fourteen months had collapsed and he was once again in that room, unable to breathe, certain he was dying. These intrusive episodes, in their vividness and bodily immediacy, reinforced his deepest fear: that his body had been permanently altered and could no longer be trusted. The taste arriving unbidden felt like evidence that something was still wrong inside him, and this conviction - that his body was unreliable - deepened each time the memory broke through.

That belief became the lens through which Thanh interpreted almost every physical sensation. He had come to feel that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, that the exposure had confirmed a fundamental helplessness he could no longer argue against. These appraisals did not remain abstract; they drove his behaviour in ways that accumulated into a recognisable pattern. He began scanning his body constantly - attending to his breathing, monitoring the back of his throat for any trace of that chemical taste, cataloguing every tightness in his chest. He also began scanning his environment with the same vigilance, checking ventilation grates, noting the smell of cleaning products, pausing at closed doors. At work, this meant that a job requiring confident, fluid movement through the hotel had become an exercise in managed dread. He would hesitate before entering storage rooms, sometimes sending junior staff ahead. Colleagues noticed. His partner noticed. Thanh, who had once moved through the building with proprietary ease, now felt like a stranger in it - a man who no longer belonged anywhere, not in his workplace, not in the body he had inhabited for sixty years.

The vigilance itself fed the very processes it was meant to contain. When Thanh scanned his body and found a sensation - a tightness, a mild throat-clearing - his nervous system treated it as confirmation of threat, flooding him with the readiness he could not turn off. His body felt perpetually braced. When a maintenance request took longer than expected to be fulfilled, he was certain something had gone wrong, that another exposure was unfolding somewhere in the building. This state of constant physiological alert made him more susceptible to the intrusive memories, which arrived with greater force when his arousal was already elevated, and each intrusion renewed his certainty that he was helpless and his body unreliable, closing the loop tightly around him.

What finally brought Thanh to seek help was a conversation with his partner, who told him quietly one evening that she was frightened - not of anything external, but of watching him disappear into himself. He came to the first session hoping, above everything, that someone could tell him his body was not still poisoned. What he feared most was that it was.
